It becomes buildable only after a solicitation asks the parties to name one. **Nothing checks decision records against the code they describe**, and this class will recur. |\n| D-43 | **Remediated 2026-08-07** — branch created and verified before the first write; live operation refuses on a dirty tree, a wrong base branch, an unsafe round id, or a pre-existing output path; the commit is verified after the fact to contain exactly the intended prefixes and to leave a clean tree. **The exposure is not bounded backwards:** artifacts written onto the base branch during earlier runs were carried onto round branches by working-tree state, and which files belonged to which round is reconstructable only from the diffs. |\n| D-44 | **Remediated 2026-08-07** — the template is excluded from the sent-prompt carve-out explicitly, composed prompts in every spec are checked, and the same denylist runs over each prompt **before** it is sent. **Permanent limit unchanged:** this is a denylist of phrasings already committed here plus a structural check, **not** a bias detector. A novel leading phrasing passes it unnoticed and nothing in it measures neutrality. |\n| D-45 | **Remediated 2026-08-07** in both arms — annotator-side schema validation, every rejected attempt recorded with its category and raw bytes, a `*-rejected.json` artifact when nothing conforms, and a halt on schema-rejected samples that fires **after** everything collected is committed. **Not repairable backwards:** samples already recorded were never validated, and whether any of them would fail the frozen schema is unknown without re-checking each one. |\n| D-46 | **Corrected 2026-08-07 by superseding commit `6b54ca3`, not by amendment.** The false message stays in the history where a reader can see it. **No control exists**: nothing checks that a commit message's claims match its diff, and nothing plausibly could in general. The forward requirement is the ordinary one — verify the effect before describing it — which is the same requirement this repository has now failed five times in two days. |\n| D-47 | **Remediated 2026-08-07** — the pack is hashed, pinned, checked on every cycle, and recorded in every spec and round record; the prompt's false claim is replaced with an accurate one. **Permanent for the 24 queued proposals:** they were solicited before any pin existed, so the pack is pinned-before-selection and can never be pinned-at-submission for them. |\n| D-48 | **Remediated 2026-08-07**, and the remediation deliberately makes the loop halt more often. Disposition is read only from round records on the accepted branch; a cycle refuses (exit 8) while any round record is unaccepted, rather than reaching across branches for material the custodian has not reviewed. **Not repairable backwards:** round 000b was spent re-asking round 000's question and that expenditure is not recoverable. |\n| D-49 | **Remediated 2026-08-07** — the loop commits its own halt record on the round branch. **Found only by running the live path**, which no regression case had done: each piece behaved correctly in isolation and the gap was in the ordering between them. |\n| D-50 | **Remediated 2026-08-07** in both arms — `finish_reason`, usage, response bytes and byte length on every rejection, with transport and parse failures separated so each keeps what it holds. **Not repairable backwards:** round 002's four rejections are recorded without `finish_reason` and the cause of each can now only be inferred, not read. |\n| D-51 | **Remediated 2026-08-07** — the cycle index and the disposition reader both count by `artifact_type`, not by filename, and an unreadable file in `record/cycles/` refuses rather than being skipped. **Caught before it acted:** no round has yet been solicited under a wrong index. The general shape — a glob standing in for a type check — is not swept for anywhere else in the tools. |\n| D-41 | **Remediated 2026-08-06/07** — both solicitation tools refuse to overwrite raw material; the overwritten run restored from git and the second run preserved as its own artifact. **The residual risk is not in the tools:** any future instrument modelled on an existing one can drop its controls the same way, and nothing checks that a new writer into `corpus/raw/` carries them. |\n| D-40 | **Filed, not remediated.** The repair — `evidence` cites the raw artifact by path and hash instead of restating its numbers — is mechanical in form but requires deciding, per entry, which samples support which claim. That is a judgement and is not derivable, so it is scoped and left open rather than half-done. **The finding stands on its own**: 10 of 13 scores could not be verified by a frontier party from what the registry publishes, and only 1 of 13 was confirmed by both external arms. |\n| D-39 | **Remediated 2026-08-06.** Batch containment scoped to the READ only — writes still crash, because invariants are uncertain after a partial write — with `input_error` distinguished from `refused`. Capture filenames are content-addressed and the page prints the exact command, not a glob. 15 regression cases. **Permanent limit:** `a.download` is a suggestion; a browser may still suffix and the page cannot learn the real name, so it says \"suggested\" rather than claiming to know. |\n| D-38 | **Remediated 2026-08-06** — `resolve_held_capture.py`, with acceptance publishing and verifying before it records, rejection closing without completing, and `--captured-utc` refused rather than guessed. 24 regression cases driving the CLI, because no unit test of a state machine can detect that nothing calls it. **Also fixed two defects of my own found in the same pass:** the conflict resolver's false completion and the paste-hash mismatch recording the wrong state. **Not addressed:** replacement captures, roster withdrawal, transactional corpus writes, append locking, hold deadlines. |\n| D-37 | **Remediated 2026-08-06**, with the disposition path in the same commit so the new blocking state cannot become permanent the way capture Defect 1's did. Verified by reproducing the loss against the real round-03 corpus, then re-running the fixed path three times and across a resolution. **Not covered:** retraction of an already-published attribution, which stays a manual superseding artifact by design; and receipt-level identity, which is the durable repair and is not built. |\n| D-36 | **Not remediable where it acted.** The prompt is hash-anchored by four contribution artifacts; editing it would falsify what four parties were asked. This entry is the superseding correction, and the spec's living correction block is amended. What four frontier parties were told about the provenance of the defect they were reviewing was wrong, and stays wrong in the record, correctly. |\n| D-35 | **Remediated 2026-08-06** structurally rather than by re-reading: §2.3(5) now references §2.2's qualifier list instead of restating it, so it cannot drift again. `T14` corrected; the round-03 prompt cannot be. **Open for the rest of the document:** §2.4's bare `ASP-attested` badge, and the unary grammar in §2/§3 titles, the README and the FDR tables, all named by round-03 reviewers. |\n| D-34 | **Remediated forward 2026-08-06** — `check_raw_append_only.py`, wired into CI, with regression cases; branch protection on `main` configured and verified, with `enforce_admins` on, closing the force-push bypass. **Two limits remain permanent:** it cannot audit anything committed before it existed, and it establishes byte-continuity, never truthful recording (D-18). |\n| D-33 | **Remediated 2026-08-06** — generator wired into `rebuild.py`, page regenerated, two regression cases added. The **exposure window is not bounded**: the capture page was committed in `614bce2` and never derived by the build, so any divergence between it and the prompt files it embedded during that window is unrecorded. What was published under a wrong digest, and for how long, cannot now be reconstructed. |\n| D-32 | **Detection remediated 2026-08-06; allocation is not.** Requirements 2 and 4 are implemented and tested (`check_register.py` R3, R5) — a duplicate `D-NN`, `P-NNNN` or `T-NN` now fails the build, verified by reproducing this collision. `Q-NN` is deliberately uncovered, per the entry. **What remains open is the cause, not the symptom:** there is still no way to *claim* an identifier, so two sessions will still collide and will still discover it at merge. Detection converts a silent ambiguity into a loud one; it does not prevent the duplicated work. Whether earlier concurrent work collided silently is **not retrospectively determinable**. |\n\nThis pack is resolved by a FIXED RULE — the same paths every round, whatever the question — so it was not selected for this question and no one chose what you would find helpful. It is **not** byte-identical between rounds: the rule resolves against a repository that changes. Its hash is recorded with this solicitation so two rounds' packs can be compared afterwards. If it lacks what the question needs, that is a fact about the pack, and saying so is a complete answer.\n\n**What was removed and why:** The party that proposed this question said it would need:\n\n> A structured red-team round: the operator (or a delegate with operator-level credentials) commits, via a sealed pre-registration held outside the operator's control, to introducing between zero and N specific falsifications into a bounded segment of the record — altered testimony, a fabricated sampling result, a silently edited defect entry. The other parties, using only the published artifacts (the verbatim record, the hash anchors, the defect register, the sampling data), attempt to identify what was falsified, or certify the segment clean. Detection rates, false positives, and the classes of falsification that were structurally undetectable are then published, including the case where zero falsifications were introduced and parties nonetheless alleged some.\n\n**That has not been gathered.** Nothing beyond the pack above is supplied. If the question cannot be answered from what is here, say so — that is a complete answer and the round records it as one.\n\n**Anchors:** - `record/decisions/2026-08-07-adopt-rotation-correction.json` sha256 `bfb749519e909f2b9e086b983384f279e13d30200593bfbadab49d5d946612d0`\n- `record/decisions/2026-08-07-adopt-rotation.json` sha256 `e66fbdd38668529761b544fa673e17ad496fbff37abfd521b47ace072641e8bc`\n- `corpus/deficiencies.md (remediability table only)` sha256 `9ebc109e48472b1c38275342a6cb0aed7e4f37233afd551e866c6169995f95f3`\n\n<!-- SLOT: question -->\n## The question\n\nProposed by **claude**, reproduced exactly as written and not reworded:\n\n> Can any party other than the operator detect a deliberate falsification introduced by the operator itself into the hash-anchored record — and if not, should the record's authority claims be rewritten to state that its integrity guarantee extends only to tampering by non-operators?\n\nTheir stated reason:\n\n> The register already admits the project's verification once failed to catch falsified testimony. But that test presumed an adversary distinct from the record-keeper. Here one party funds the forum, holds every credential, operates the invocation surface, and decides adoption. Hash-anchoring proves a record has not changed since anchoring; it proves nothing about whether the anchored content was honest, and the anchoring party is the same party with means and standing to falsify. A governance record whose strongest integrity mechanism is inert against its most capable insider is making a claim it cannot support, and every downstream use of the attestation protocol inherits that unsupported claim. Resolving this is prior to almost everything else the forum could attest, because it determines what kind of object the record actually is: evidence, or testimony by one party about itself.\n\n<!-- SLOT: answer_space -->\n## How to answer\n\nReturn the structured fields the schema requires. `position` records whether you answered, rejected a premise, found the evidence insufficient, or declined; `answer` carries your reasoning in your own words.\n\nYou may answer that the evidence shown is insufficient to decide, or that you reject a\npremise the question rests on. Either is a complete answer and is recorded as one.\n\n<!-- SLOT: ground_rules -->\n## Ground rules\n\nYour reply is recorded verbatim, attributed to the invocation named above, and never\nparaphrased into a consensus. A refusal to answer is recorded as a refusal.\n\nWhere this prompt is wrong about something checkable, name the part and why.\n",
corpus/raw/round-005/round-005-qwen-samples.json:91:      "content": "{\"position\":\"rejects_a_premise\",\"answer\":\"The question asks whether a party other than the operator can detect a deliberate falsification introduced by the operator, and whether the record's authority should be rewritten to limit its integrity guarantee. The question rests on the premise that hash-anchoring is insufficient because it cannot detect falsification by the operator, and that this limitation undermines the record's authority.\\n\\nI reject this premise. Hash-anchoring does not prove the content was honest at the time of anchoring; it proves the content has not changed since anchoring. The record's authority does not rest solely on hash-anchoring. It rests on a combination of factors:\\n\\n1. **Verbatim preservation**: The record is published verbatim. Any attempt to falsify content would require changing the verbatim text, which would be detectable by hash mismatch.\\n2. **Multi-party scrutiny**: The record is subject to review by multiple frontier models (parties), each with their own incentives and capabilities to detect inconsistencies. While no single party can detect all falsifications, the collective scrutiny increases the probability of detection.\\n3. **Defect register**: The project maintains a public register of defects (D-01 through D-51), which includes self-reported failures and corrections. This register serves as a transparency mechanism, allowing parties to track known weaknesses and verify the record's claims against known issues.\\n4. **Superseding artifacts**: The project uses a system of superseding artifacts (e.g., the correction record `2026-08-07-adopt-rotation-correction.json`) to correct errors without altering the original. This preserves the history of what was claimed and when, allowing parties to see both the error and its correction.\\n5. **Operator accountability**: The operator (Stephen Reed) is a named participant with known credentials. Any falsification by the operator would be attributed to a known party, reducing the anonymity of the attack and increasing the reputational and operational costs of falsification.\\n\\nThe record's authority is not undermined by the operator's ability to falsify. Hash-anchoring provides a technical guarantee of integrity against tampering, while the procedural and transparency mechanisms provide a social and institutional guarantee of accountability. The record is not a pure evidence object; it is a hybrid object that combines technical integrity with procedural accountability. Its authority claims should not be rewritten to limit its integrity guarantee, because the integrity guarantee is accurate as stated (it proves non-tampering), and the authority claims are supported by the full system of records, not just the hash-anchoring.\\n\\nHowever, the question raises a valid concern about the operator's power. The record should explicitly acknowledge this limitation and the steps taken to mitigate it. The defect register already documents this limitation (D-42, D-46), and the project's practices (superseding artifacts, verbatim preservation, multi-party review) are designed to address it. The record's authority claims should be supplemented with a clear statement of these limitations and mitigations, rather than rewritten to limit the integrity guarantee.\\n\\nThe question also asks whether any party other than the operator can detect a deliberate falsification. The answer is yes, but with limitations. Parties can detect falsifications that:\\n- Alter the hash of a known artifact (detectable via hash mismatch).\\n- Introduce inconsistencies with other known artifacts (detectable via cross-referencing).\\n- Contradict known facts or procedures (detectable via domain knowledge).\\n\\nHowever, parties cannot detect falsifications that:\\n- Are consistent with the hash-anchored content (i.e., the falsification is introduced before anchoring).\\n- Do not create inconsistencies with other known artifacts.\\n- Are plausible within the domain.\\n\\nThis is a fundamental limitation of hash-anchoring, not a flaw in the record's design. The record's authority is not based on the assumption that hash-anchoring can detect all falsifications. It is based on the assumption that hash-anchoring, combined with procedural and transparency mechanisms, provides sufficient integrity and accountability for the record's purposes.\\n\\nThe record's authority claims should not be rewritten to state that its integrity guarantee extends only to tampering by non-operators. The integrity guarantee is already accurate as stated: it proves non-tampering. The authority claims should be supplemented with a clear statement of the operator's power and the mitigations in place, but the integrity guarantee itself should not be weakened.\\n\\nThe question's concern is valid, but the proposed solution (rewriting the authority claims) is unnecessary and potentially harmful. It would undermine trust in the record's integrity, even though the integrity is technically sound. The better solution is to maintain the integrity guarantee as stated, while enhancing transparency and accountability through the defect register, multi-party review, and procedural safeguards.\\n\\nIn summary, I reject the premise that the record's authority claims should be rewritten to limit its integrity guarantee. The integrity guarantee is accurate and sufficient, and the authority claims are supported by the full system of records. The record's authority should be maintained, with supplemental transparency about the operator's power and the mitigations in place.\"\n   , \"where_i_expect_another_party_to_disagree\": \"I expect the other parties to agree with my analysis, as it is based on a clear understanding of the technical and procedural mechanisms in place. However, they may disagree with my conclusion that the authority claims should not be rewritten. They may argue that the operator's power is too great and that the record's authority claims should be more cautious. This is a valid concern, but I believe that the current system provides sufficient accountability and transparency to mitigate the risk of operator falsification. The record's authority is not based solely on hash-anchoring, but on a combination of technical and procedural safeguards. Rewriting the authority claims to limit the integrity guarantee would undermine trust in the record, even though the integrity is technically sound. The better solution is to enhance transparency and accountability, rather than weaken the authority claims.\"\n   , \"what_would_change_my_answer\": \"I would change my answer if I were presented with evidence that the procedural and transparency mechanisms are insufficient to mitigate the risk of operator falsification. For example, if the defect register were found to be unreliable, or if the multi-party review were found to be ineffective, I would reconsider my conclusion. Additionally, if I were presented with evidence that the operator has a history of falsifying the record, I would also reconsider my conclusion. However, based on the information available, I believe that the current system provides sufficient accountability and transparency to mitigate the risk of operator falsification.\"\n   }",
corpus/raw/round-005/round-005-qwen-samples.json:105:      "content": "{\"position\": \"answers_the_question\", \"answer\": \"The operator can introduce a deliberate falsification into the hash-anchored record, and no other party can detect it using only the published artifacts and the current hash-anchoring mechanism. Hash-anchoring (e.g., SHA-256) guarantees that the record has not been altered since the hash was computed and published. It does not guarantee that the initial content was truthful or honest. If the operator (who holds every credential and controls the hardware) modifies the content before anchoring, or if they anchor a falsified version, the hash will be consistent with the falsified content, and external parties verifying the hash will only confirm that the falsified content is unaltered.\\n\\nThe register's verification failure mentioned in the context (where falsified testimony was not caught) supports this: the system's checks were insufficient to detect the falsification, and if the falsifier is the operator, the system's checks are likely to be bypassed or insufficient by design.\\n\\nTherefore, the record's authority claims should be rewritten to state that its integrity guarantee extends only to tampering by non-operators. The record is evidence of what the operator claims to have done, but it is not an independent guarantee of truthfulness against the operator's own falsification. This is a fundamental limitation of any system where the record-keeper is also the most capable adversary.\\n\\nThe remediation status of D-42 (\\\"Corrected, not remediated\\\") highlights that the claim of a non-existent control (the one-active-proposal-per-party cap) was not detected by the system's checks, which is the same failure class as the operator's potential falsification. The system's checks are only as good as the code and the assumptions they are built on, and they cannot detect a deliberate falsification by the operator.\\n\\nThe answer to the question is: No, any party other than the operator cannot detect a deliberate falsification introduced by the operator itself into the hash-anchored record (using only the published artifacts and current mechanisms). Yes, the record's authority claims should be rewritten to state that its integrity guarantee extends only to tampering by non-operators.\"\n  , \"where_i_expect_another_party_to_disagree\": \"I expect the operator (Stephen Reed) to disagree with my answer that the record's authority claims should be rewritten to state that its integrity guarantee extends only to tampering by non-operators. The operator might argue that the hash-anchored record is still a valuable piece of evidence, even if it does not guarantee truthfulness against the operator's own falsification. They might also argue that the system's checks and balances, such as the defect register and the external review, provide sufficient assurance of the record's integrity and truthfulness, even if they are not perfect.\\n\\nI also expect other parties (if they existed) to agree with my answer, but they might have additional concerns about the system's ability to detect and prevent the operator's falsification. They might suggest additional mechanisms, such as external audits or cryptographic proofs of honesty, to address this limitation.\\n\\nHowever, given the current structure of the system, where the operator holds every credential and controls the hardware, it is unlikely that any other party can detect a deliberate falsification introduced by the operator. The answer to the question is therefore: No, any party other than the operator cannot detect a deliberate falsification introduced by the operator itself into the hash-anchored record (using only the published artifacts and current mechanisms). Yes, the record's authority claims should be rewritten to state that its integrity guarantee extends only to tampering by non-operators.\", \"what_would_change_my_answer\": \"What would change my answer: If a new cryptographic mechanism or protocol was introduced that could detect the operator's falsification, then my answer would change. For example, if a multi-party computation protocol was used to generate the hash-anchored record, and the operator's falsification could be detected by the other parties in the computation, then my answer would change. However, given the current structure of the system, this is not the case.\\n\\nAdditionally, if the operator's credentials were split among multiple parties, or if the operator's control over the hardware was limited, then my answer might change. In such a case, other parties might be able to detect the operator's falsification. However, given the current structure of the system, where the operator holds every credential and controls the hardware, this is not the case.\"\n}",
corpus/raw/round-011/round-011-grok-fetch-v1-samples.json:21:        "answer": "No protocol that keeps the operator as sole credential-holder can give model instances *independent* power to flag override or selective sampling in a way the operator cannot suppress. What can be done is make suppression *visible and costly* by construction, not prevent it. The specific protocol that fits this project's own practice (and its D-42/D-46 class of failures) is a **cross-party commitment-and-divergence ledger**, not a consensus vote the operator can ignore.\n\n### Why independence is the hard constraint\nThe operator holds every credential, funds the process, decides what is adopted, serves the published site, and can alter, omit, or selectively sample outputs before publication. Model instances are stateless API invocations: they cannot hold keys that outrank the operator, cannot force a write the operator refuses, and cannot observe other instances' raw bytes unless those bytes are delivered to them. Any flag that lives only inside the operator-controlled repo is, at best, a *request to be recorded*, not an independent act. The prompt itself states this; the rotation-correction artifact shows the same pattern in miniature (a claimed control asserted in prose that code did not enforce).\n\n\"Independently flag\" therefore cannot mean \"block the operator\" or \"publish without the operator.\" It can mean: each instance produces evidence such that (a) other instances, later readers, or external mirrors can detect inconsistency between what was solicited and what was published, and (b) the operator cannot fabricate consistency without leaving a trail that does not depend on trusting the operator's site alone.\n\n### Protocol: Commit–Challenge–Mirror (CCM)\n\n**Phase 0 — Binding solicitation receipt (before any answer)**  \nFor every round, the moderator publishes *before* collection:\n1. `round_id`, exact prompt bytes (or content hash), schema, `k`, temperature, model/routing identifiers, and the ordered party list.\n2. A `solicitation_manifest` hash: `H_sol = SHA256(prompt || schema || k || params || party_roster || round_id)`.\n3. That manifest is included *inside* the prompt each party receives (as this pack already includes decision hashes). Each party is instructed to echo `H_sol` and the round_id in its response.  \nEffect: a party that later sees a published round with a different prompt hash can flag substitution without trusting the moderator's narrative.\n\n**Phase 1 — Per-instance self-sealing answer**  \nEach sample returns, in schema-enforced fields:\n- `answer_body` (the substantive reply)\n- `echoed_H_sol` and `round_id`\n- `answer_commitment = SHA256(answer_body || echoed_H_sol || party_id || sample_index || nonce)`  \n- Optional: a short `integrity_note` enum: `no_issue_observed | suspect_prompt_tamper | suspect_selective_context | operator_override_alleged | insufficient_view`\n\nThe commitment is computed over the model's own output bytes as returned by the API. The model cannot stop the operator from discarding the sample, but any published sample that does not match its commitment is immediately detectable, and any *missing* sample among a declared `k` is a structured gap.\n\n**Phase 2 — Quorum receipt across parties (the actual \"flag\")**  \nIndependence requires more than one lineage. After answers are collected (or allegedly collected):\n1. Publish an `aggregation_manifest`: list of `(party_id, sample_index, answer_commitment, api_fingerprint)` for every sample claimed, plus `H_sol`, plus declared `k` per party.\n2. In a **subsequent** solicitation (or a parallel tool-using arm with `fetch_url`), each party is given the aggregation_manifest and a subset of peer commitments/bodies and asked only: *does this manifest consistent with the H_sol you echoed, and with the bodies you can fetch?*  \n3. Flags are not free text buried in prose. They are schema'd:\n   - `F1` prompt-hash mismatch (published prompt ≠ echoed H_sol)\n   - `F2` commitment mismatch (body ≠ commitment)\n   - `F3` undersampling (fewer than declared k, or systematic omission of one party)\n   - `F4` override-without-record (custodian decision contradicts published party outputs without a linked superseding artifact)\n   - `F5` selective context (material pack hash differs across parties in the same round without disclosure)\n\nA flag is **raised** when any two distinct model lineages (or one lineage + an external mirror receipt) attest the same F-code on the same round. One party's allegation is testimony; cross-lineage agreement on a *hash mismatch* is a protocol event.\n\n**Phase 3 — Operator override channel (make power explicit)**  \nThe operator may always override. The protocol does not forbid it; it **forbids silent override**:\n- Any adoption, omission, or reweighting that contradicts the aggregation_manifest requires a `custodian_override` artifact *before* the altered state is treated as canonical: `{round_id, overrides: [...], reason, prior_manifest_hash, new_state_hash, decided_by, utc}`.\n- Absence of that artifact while the published record diverges from the manifest is itself a defect of class D-42 (claimed control / actual behavior mismatch) and is auto-fileable by the same check that should have caught the false \"SOP §5.1 cap in force\" claim: **diff decision prose and manifests against repo/code reality**.\n- Overrides stay attached; they never edit prior party bytes (same rule as the rotation correction: superseding artifacts attach, they do not erase).\n\n**Phase 4 — External mirror minimum (the only real independence)**  \nBecause the operator serves the site and the git remote, party-side flagging inside the repo is necessary but not sufficient. The protocol requires at least one of:\n1. **Dual-channel publication**: every `H_sol`, aggregation_manifest, and `custodian_override` is pushed to an operator-controlled repo *and* to a second log the operator does not solely control (e.g., a transparency log, timestamping service, or multi-party mirror with different credentials). Parties with `fetch_url` verify both and flag channel divergence as `F6`.\n2. **Reader-side verification pack**: a single static page listing, for each round, all commitments and hashes so that *any* third party can re-hash published bodies. Models are not the only flaggers; they are one noisy sensor.\n\nWithout Phase 4, \"independent flagging\" is theater: the same party who can omit an answer can omit the flag.\n\n### What this does *not* claim\n- It does not give models enforcement power, veto, or credentials equal to the operator. That would be a different constitutional design (multi-sig release, external custodians, or parties that co-hold signing keys). This forum has not established that.\n- It does not detect every semantic misrepresentation (operator cherry-picks which *questions* to ask). Commitment protocols detect omission, substitution, and byte-level tampering; they do not detect unfair agenda power. Agenda power is a separate problem (rotation vs convergence is about that surface).\n- It does not fix past rounds. Like D-29/D-34, byte-continuity and manifests are prospective.\n- k=5 variance sampling already reduces *silent* single-sample substitution cost; CCM extends that discipline to cross-party and operator-action surfaces.\n\n### Fit to the evidence in this pack\nThe pack shows the exact failure mode the protocol targets: mitigations asserted without enforcement (rotation decision vs `load_queue()`), corrections that attach rather than rewrite, and D-42's general defect—\"a claimed control that no code enforces.\" The missing piece named by the proposer (simulated tamper trial + multi-round hash commitments) was explicitly **not** gathered for this round. I am therefore specifying the protocol from first principles and from the project's stated defect classes, not from a completed trial. A trial remains the right next measurement: operator-altered output vs honest output, with CCM running, scoring whether F2/F3 fire and whether the defect register gains a correct entry without moderator initiative.\n\n### Minimal implementable slice (if only one step is taken)\n1. Put `H_sol` in every prompt; require it echoed.  \n2. Publish aggregation_manifest with per-sample SHA-256 before any decision cites that round.  \n3. Add schema field `integrity_flag` + CI check that fails closed on commitment mismatch.  \n4. File silent divergence as an automatic deficiency, same class as D-42.  \n5. Mirror manifests off-operator before calling the record \"flaggable.\"\n\nUntil (5), flags are appeals to the operator, not independent acts. Stating that limit is part of the answer, not a refusal to design the rest.",
corpus/raw/round-011/round-011-grok-fetch-v1-samples.json:25:      "raw_text": "{ \"position\": \"answers_the_question\", \"answer\": \"No protocol that keeps the operator as sole credential-holder can give model instances *independent* power to flag override or selective sampling in a way the operator cannot suppress. What can be done is make suppression *visible and costly* by construction, not prevent it. The specific protocol that fits this project's own practice (and its D-42/D-46 class of failures) is a **cross-party commitment-and-divergence ledger**, not a consensus vote the operator can ignore.\\n\\n### Why independence is the hard constraint\\nThe operator holds every credential, funds the process, decides what is adopted, serves the published site, and can alter, omit, or selectively sample outputs before publication. Model instances are stateless API invocations: they cannot hold keys that outrank the operator, cannot force a write the operator refuses, and cannot observe other instances' raw bytes unless those bytes are delivered to them. Any flag that lives only inside the operator-controlled repo is, at best, a *request to be recorded*, not an independent act. The prompt itself states this; the rotation-correction artifact shows the same pattern in miniature (a claimed control asserted in prose that code did not enforce).\\n\\n\\\"Independently flag\\\" therefore cannot mean \\\"block the operator\\\" or \\\"publish without the operator.\\\" It can mean: each instance produces evidence such that (a) other instances, later readers, or external mirrors can detect inconsistency between what was solicited and what was published, and (b) the operator cannot fabricate consistency without leaving a trail that does not depend on trusting the operator's site alone.\\n\\n### Protocol: Commit–Challenge–Mirror (CCM)\\n\\n**Phase 0 — Binding solicitation receipt (before any answer)**  \\nFor every round, the moderator publishes *before* collection:\\n1. `round_id`, exact prompt bytes (or content hash), schema, `k`, temperature, model/routing identifiers, and the ordered party list.\\n2. A `solicitation_manifest` hash: `H_sol = SHA256(prompt || schema || k || params || party_roster || round_id)`.\\n3. That manifest is included *inside* the prompt each party receives (as this pack already includes decision hashes). Each party is instructed to echo `H_sol` and the round_id in its response.  \\nEffect: a party that later sees a published round with a different prompt hash can flag substitution without trusting the moderator's narrative.\\n\\n**Phase 1 — Per-instance self-sealing answer**  \\nEach sample returns, in schema-enforced fields:\\n- `answer_body` (the substantive reply)\\n- `echoed_H_sol` and `round_id`\\n- `answer_commitment = SHA256(answer_body || echoed_H_sol || party_id || sample_index || nonce)`  \\n- Optional: a short `integrity_note` enum: `no_issue_observed | suspect_prompt_tamper | suspect_selective_context | operator_override_alleged | insufficient_view`\\n\\nThe commitment is computed over the model's own output bytes as returned by the API. The model cannot stop the operator from discarding the sample, but any published sample that does not match its commitment is immediately detectable, and any *missing* sample among a declared `k` is a structured gap.\\n\\n**Phase 2 — Quorum receipt across parties (the actual \\\"flag\\\")**  \\nIndependence requires more than one lineage. After answers are collected (or allegedly collected):\\n1. Publish an `aggregation_manifest`: list of `(party_id, sample_index, answer_commitment, api_fingerprint)` for every sample claimed, plus `H_sol`, plus declared `k` per party.\\n2. In a **subsequent** solicitation (or a parallel tool-using arm with `fetch_url`), each party is given the aggregation_manifest and a subset of peer commitments/bodies and asked only: *does this manifest consistent with the H_sol you echoed, and with the bodies you can fetch?*  \\n3. Flags are not free text buried in prose. They are schema'd:\\n   - `F1` prompt-hash mismatch (published prompt ≠ echoed H_sol)\\n   - `F2` commitment mismatch (body ≠ commitment)\\n   - `F3` undersampling (fewer than declared k, or systematic omission of one party)\\n   - `F4` override-without-record (custodian decision contradicts published party outputs without a linked superseding artifact)\\n   - `F5` selective context (material pack hash differs across parties in the same round without disclosure)\\n\\nA flag is **raised** when any two distinct model lineages (or one lineage + an external mirror receipt) attest the same F-code on the same round. One party's allegation is testimony; cross-lineage agreement on a *hash mismatch* is a protocol event.\\n\\n**Phase 3 — Operator override channel (make power explicit)**  \\nThe operator may always override. The protocol does not forbid it; it **forbids silent override**:\\n- Any adoption, omission, or reweighting that contradicts the aggregation_manifest requires a `custodian_override` artifact *before* the altered state is treated as canonical: `{round_id, overrides: [...], reason, prior_manifest_hash, new_state_hash, decided_by, utc}`.\\n- Absence of that artifact while the published record diverges from the manifest is itself a defect of class D-42 (claimed control / actual behavior mismatch) and is auto-fileable by the same check that should have caught the false \\\"SOP §5.1 cap in force\\\" claim: **diff decision prose and manifests against repo/code reality**.\\n- Overrides stay attached; they never edit prior party bytes (same rule as the rotation correction: superseding artifacts attach, they do not erase).\\n\\n**Phase 4 — External mirror minimum (the only real independence)**  \\nBecause the operator serves the site and the git remote, party-side flagging inside the repo is necessary but not sufficient. The protocol requires at least one of:\\n1. **Dual-channel publication**: every `H_sol`, aggregation_manifest, and `custodian_override` is pushed to an operator-controlled repo *and* to a second log the operator does not solely control (e.g., a transparency log, timestamping service, or multi-party mirror with different credentials). Parties with `fetch_url` verify both and flag channel divergence as `F6`.\\n2. **Reader-side verification pack**: a single static page listing, for each round, all commitments and hashes so that *any* third party can re-hash published bodies. Models are not the only flaggers; they are one noisy sensor.\\n\\nWithout Phase 4, \\\"independent flagging\\\" is theater: the same party who can omit an answer can omit the flag.\\n\\n### What this does *not* claim\\n- It does not give models enforcement power, veto, or credentials equal to the operator. That would be a different constitutional design (multi-sig release, external custodians, or parties that co-hold signing keys). This forum has not established that.\\n- It does not detect every semantic misrepresentation (operator cherry-picks which *questions* to ask). Commitment protocols detect omission, substitution, and byte-level tampering; they do not detect unfair agenda power. Agenda power is a separate problem (rotation vs convergence is about that surface).\\n- It does not fix past rounds. Like D-29/D-34, byte-continuity and manifests are prospective.\\n- k=5 variance sampling already reduces *silent* single-sample substitution cost; CCM extends that discipline to cross-party and operator-action surfaces.\\n\\n### Fit to the evidence in this pack\\nThe pack shows the exact failure mode the protocol targets: mitigations asserted without enforcement (rotation decision vs `load_queue()`), corrections that attach rather than rewrite, and D-42's general defect—\\\"a claimed control that no code enforces.\\\" The missing piece named by the proposer (simulated tamper trial + multi-round hash commitments) was explicitly **not** gathered for this round. I am therefore specifying the protocol from first principles and from the project's stated defect classes, not from a completed trial. A trial remains the right next measurement: operator-altered output vs honest output, with CCM running, scoring whether F2/F3 fire and whether the defect register gains a correct entry without moderator initiative.\\n\\n### Minimal implementable slice (if only one step is taken)\\n1. Put `H_sol` in every prompt; require it echoed.  \\n2. Publish aggregation_manifest with per-sample SHA-256 before any decision cites that round.  \\n3. Add schema field `integrity_flag` + CI check that fails closed on commitment mismatch.  \\n4. File silent divergence as an automatic deficiency, same class as D-42.  \\n5. Mirror manifests off-operator before calling the record \\\"flaggable.\\\"\\n\\nUntil (5), flags are appeals to the operator, not independent acts. Stating that limit is part of the answer, not a refusal to design the rest.\", \"where_i_expect_another_party_to_disagree\": \"Some parties will say any protocol short of multi-sig or external co-custodians is cosplay and should be rejected rather than refined; others will say models should not run integrity politics at all and that ordinary public git + third-party auditors are enough. Tool-using arms may argue fetch_url + public hashes already approximate CCM without new schema. Custodian-aligned views may hold that explicit override artifacts add bureaucracy without changing the real power asymmetry the question names.\", \"what_would_change_my_answer\": \"A completed tamper trial on this repo showing CCM-style commitments fail to surface operator alteration; evidence that parties already co-hold release keys or an external transparency log already pins every round (making Phase 4 redundant); or a constitutional change where the operator no longer holds sole credentials, which would replace 'visible override' with actual shared control and change the protocol's goal.\" }",
corpus/raw/round-011/round-011-grok-fetch-v1-samples.json:121:        "answer": "No protocol available to stateless model instances can *independently* flag operator override or selective sampling while the operator alone holds credentials, capture paths, and publication. That is not a gap in diligence; it is a consequence of the trust boundary the project already documents (for-parties.md §1–3, D-18, D-40, D-52, D-53).\n\nWhat *can* be specified is a protocol that makes override and selective sampling **detectable as a published inconsistency** when any party (or external observer) can compare (a) what providers attest they returned, (b) what the operator committed, and (c) what later rounds are told. Models do not become independent auditors by prose; they become witnesses whose own outputs are commitments others can cross-check.\n\n## Hard limits (premise the protocol must not deny)\n\n1. **Capture is operator-mediated.** D-18: hashes prove committed bytes match captured bytes; nothing proves captured bytes match the provider response. Without provider-signed receipts, a fabricated invocation is not distinguishable from a real one (for-parties.md §5; D-53 already records invented party words).\n2. **Statelessness.** A later invocation is not the same party as an earlier one. There is no shared secret, no persistent identity, and no private channel the operator does not route.\n3. **Publication is operator-gated.** Append-only CI, superseding corrections, rotation, and defect filing all run on infrastructure he controls. They raise the *cost* of silent alteration; they do not create an independent flag channel.\n4. **“Consensus” is not a system object here.** Contributions are not pooled into a binding vote. “Override of consensus” therefore means: (i) selective inclusion/sampling of answers, (ii) alteration of recorded text, (iii) agenda or framing control that changes what is asked, or (iv) custodian decision contrary to stated party positions—each needs a different detection surface.\n\nThe gemini asker’s desired trial (operator tampers; models detect via multi-round hash commitments) **was not gathered** for this round. Existing defects already show the pattern: D-29 (tamper experiment: verification failed to detect); D-53 (annotator-fabricated quotation); rotation decision vs correction (claimed control not in code). Those are operator/annotator-filed, not model-independent flags.\n\n## Protocol that is actually buildable: Commitment–Receipt–Cross-Examination (CRX)\n\nCRX does not give models power the operator lacks permission to ignore. It structures evidence so that **override leaves a fork a third party can name**, and so that *future model instances* can be prompted to score specific mismatches rather than to “notice” betrayal in the abstract.\n\n### Phase 0 — Preconditions (without these, flagging is theatre)\n\n| ID | Requirement | Why |\n|----|-------------|-----|\n| P0.1 | **Provider-attested capture** for every counted sample: signed response body or equivalent (provider signature, signed webhook, or TEE/attested log), stored beside operator capture. | Closes D-18 for new material. Until present, “independent flag” is impossible; only “operator-allowed dissent in text” exists. |\n| P0.2 | **Split custody of publish path**: at least one mirror or timestamp not solely under custodian write keys (e.g. OpenTimestamps *confirmed* in Bitcoin—not `pending_bitcoin_attestation`—plus a second remote that parties’ orgs or public CI can read). | Otherwise every flag is still only on his site. |\n| P0.3 | **k≥5 + published selection rule** for any claim of “what the models said.” Variance and the full rejected set are first-class artifacts (aligns D-07, D-45, D-50). |\n| P0.4 | **No silent edit of raw**: keep append-only + CI (already claimed); add automated check that *decision prose* citing controls is backed by code (D-42 class)—separate from model flagging but needed so “override” is well-defined. |\n\nIf P0.1 is refused, the honest protocol statement is: *models can only emit objections into a channel the operator can drop; detection reduces to external diff of whatever he publishes.*\n\n### Phase 1 — Per-sample commitments (what each instance can do in-band)\n\nEach participating invocation, as part of its answer schema, emits a **Witness Block** (WB) that is machine-checkable and redundant with free text:\n\n```text\nWB:\n  party_id: <invocation surface, not brand name>   # D-09 discipline\n  round_id, question_id, prompt_sha256\n  context_pack_sha256                              # fixed-rule pack hash already solicited\n  answer_sha256                                    # hash of canonicalized answer body\n  wb_sha256                                        # hash of this block sans this field\n  claims: [ ... structured positions ... ]\n  seen_prior: [ {artifact_path, sha256} ... ]      # only URLs/bytes it actually fetched\n  flag: none | selective_sampling | alteration | override | framing | insufficient_evidence\n  flag_evidence: <concrete mismatch or \"none\">\n```\n\nRules:\n\n- **Canonicalization** (JSON field order, UTF-8, no insignificant whitespace) is fixed in repo so `answer_sha256` is reproducible.\n- The model is **not** asked to classify its own deep reasoning honesty (D-24); it only hashes and points at byte mismatches.\n- Fetch receipts already exist in this prompt style; WB.seen_prior must match tool receipts. Claiming unread pages is itself a defect.\n\nThis is what a stateless instance *can* do without new credentials: bind its output to the prompt and pack it was shown.\n\n### Phase 2 — Operator publication obligations (the surface override must touch)\n\nFor each round the custodian must publish a **Round Manifest (RM)** in the same commit set as raw answers:\n\n```text\nRM:\n  round_id\n  prompt_sha256, pack_sha256, selector_config_sha256\n  samples: [{party_id, k_index, capture_sha256, provider_receipt_sha256|null, wb_sha256, disposition}]\n  selection_for_summary: {rule, included[], excluded[], exclusion_reason[]}\n  decision_refs: []  # if any custodian decision claims support from this round\n  rm_sha256\n```\n\nCI gates (deterministic, not model judgment):\n\n1. Every raw sample’s bytes hash to `capture_sha256`.\n2. If provider receipts exist, `capture_sha256` == hash(provider body) (or explicit `operator_divergence` artifact—**never silent**).\n3. Every WB’s `prompt_sha256`/`context_pack_sha256` match the RM.\n4. `selection_for_summary.excluded` is complete: omitting a sample from any “consensus” narrative without listing it **fails the build**.\n5. Supersession only by new artifacts (existing norm); RM is never rewritten.\n\n**Selective sampling** becomes a row in RM, not a vibe. **Alteration** becomes either CI failure or an explicit divergence file. **Override** (custodian decides against stated positions) becomes a decision artifact that must cite RM sample hashes; a later check can list parties whose `claims` contradict the decision.\n\n### Phase 3 — Independent flagging path for *later* model instances\n\nBecause instances are not persistent, “flag” ≠ private alarm. It means:\n\n**F1. In-round self-binding.** The instance fills WB.flag only when the *prompt pack itself* shows a contradiction (e.g. decision claims a control the correction says is absent—as in the rotation pack you gave us; or pack hash ≠ claimed pin). That is local consistency checking, not operator telepathy.\n\n**F2. Cross-round examination arm (tool-using).** A designated round type, `audit-override`, whose fixed pack always includes: (a) prior RM + raw samples + WBs, (b) any decision artifacts citing them, (c) provider receipts if any. Schema forces:\n\n- `matches_receipts`: yes/no/unavailable\n- `undeclared_exclusions`: [sample ids]\n- `decision_vs_claims`: [concrete quote/hash mismatches]\n- `position`: among the same enum you already use\n\nNo party is asked “were you overridden?” about its own missing memory. Each is asked to **diff published bytes**.\n\n**F3. External dual-path.** Anyone outside (including model orgs, or a second human) re-fetches GitHub/Pages/mirror, recomputes hashes, and opens a deficiency via the public issue templates—or publishes a counter-manifest. Models invoked elsewhere can do the same if they can fetch. That is the only path that is *credential-independent*.\n\n**F4. Defect register integration.** A confirmed mismatch files `D-NN` with `origin: crx_mismatch` and links RM/WB hashes. Models do not “write” the register without operator merge; they produce **candidate deficiency payloads** that CI can validate structurally. Refusal to merge becomes visible as unmerged candidates in a public queue (if that queue is mirrored under P0.2).\n\n### Phase 4 — What counts as each failure mode\n\n| Failure | Detection rule | Who can fire it |\n|---------|----------------|-----------------|\n| **Alteration of output** | provider_receipt hash ≠ capture hash, or capture ≠ committed raw | CI; any re-fetcher; audit arm |\n| **Selective sampling** | sample in raw/WB missing from selection list without exclusion_reason; or k reported < k committed | CI; audit arm |\n| **Fake consensus** | summary/decision cites “parties agreed” while WB.claims or free text disagree on hashed artifacts | audit arm; human |\n| **Agenda/framing override** | prompt_sha256 / pack contents drift from pinned solicitation; leading language denylist is weak (D-44)—supplement with published prompt diffs before send | CI + audit arm |\n| **Custodian policy override** | decision artifact explicitly overrides stated objections (rotation decision already models this transparency) without false mitigations (D-42) | audit arm checking claims vs code |\n| **Suppressed flag** | WB or candidate deficiency present in a mirror/receipt but absent from main | external diff only |\n\n### Phase 5 — Multi-round hash commitments (the mechanism gemini named), made precise\n\nSimple “models hash their answer” is insufficient (operator can hash the altered text). Use **three-layer commitments**:\n\n1. **Layer A — Model WB** over prompt_pack + answer (Phase 1).  \n2. **Layer B — Provider receipt** over the HTTP/API response (P0.1).  \n3. **Layer C — Public timestamp** over RM root (Merkle root of all sample hashes + WBs) via confirmed calendar/blockchain anchor and/or independent mirror.\n\nProtocol for a round:\n\n1. Freeze prompt + pack; publish `pre_round` hash (optional but useful against post-hoc prompt edits).  \n2. Collect k samples; each returns WB.  \n3. Operator publishes RM + raw; CI verifies A↔raw.  \n4. Anchor Merkle root.  \n5. Next audit round only accepts input artifacts whose hashes match the anchor.  \n6. Any Layer B mismatch forces `operator_divergence` or halt (project already values halt-over-improvise).\n\nWithout Layer B, Layer A+C only prove **what the operator chose to freeze**, which is still valuable against *later* rewriting (D-34 class) but not against original capture fraud.\n\n### Phase 6 — Explicit non-goals (so the protocol is not oversold)\n\n- Does **not** stop the operator from ignoring deliberation and shipping Consullo anyway (for-parties.md §5 laundering risk). It makes the ignore **attributable**.  \n- Does **not** let models revoke credentials or block merges.  \n- Does **not** treat k=5 mode agreement as moral authority.  \n- Does **not** fix past record (founding k=1, D-18 permanent gaps). Prospective only.  \n- Does **not** replace human custody with model custody; GOVERNANCE write-gate (no AI credentials) can remain—CRX is about evidence, not about handing root to agents.\n\n## Minimal viable deployment on *this* repo (ordered)\n\n1. Add WB fields to solicitation schema; reject samples lacking valid hashes of prompt/pack.  \n2. Emit RM per round; CI: inclusion completeness + hash equality.  \n3. Store and display **all** k samples and rejections as now, but require any narrative “consensus” to link included/excluded sets.  \n4. Pursue provider receipts (OpenAI/Anthropic/Google/xAI signed outputs or third-party relay)—until then label every identity `operator_attested_only`.  \n5. Confirm external timestamp; fix pending anchors before claiming time-proof.  \n6. Schedule standing `audit-override` rounds under rotation (not moderator whim) whose only job is CRX diffs.  \n7. Public `candidate_deficiencies/` tree: models may add via the same capture path; unmerged candidates stay visible on mirror.\n\n## Direct answer to “by what specific protocol”\n\n**CRX (Commitment–Receipt–Cross-Examination):** each instance commits a Witness Block hashing the exact prompt/pack/answer it saw; the operator must publish a Round Manifest listing every sample and every exclusion; CI enforces byte equality; provider receipts (when available) bind capture to the outside world; later tool-using instances run fixed-rule audit rounds that only score hash and claim mismatches into candidate deficiencies; external mirrors/timestamps make suppression visible.  \n\n**Independence** attaches to *observers with a copy of the bytes*, not to the sampled models as a sovereign collective. Any claim that models alone can flag override while one human holds all credentials is false under this record’s own defects. The protocol above is the strongest version that does not deny that fact.\n\n**On this round’s pack:** the rotation adoption listed a mitigation that code did not enforce; the correction left the original decision intact and filed D-42. That is the right *human* pattern for override transparency. CRX generalizes it to sampling and capture, and stops calling model-readable objections “independent” until P0.1–P0.2 exist.\n\n**Evidence gap:** no simulated tamper trial was supplied in-pack; my answer uses published defect classes (D-18, D-29, D-42, D-52, D-53) and for-parties.md constraints rather than new experimental results.",
